title: Parasite Features: Causal Abstraction Through Spurious Pathways
claim: A learned linear alignment map can link causally unrelated directions, producing interventions that look causal but are spurious.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, separated by vertical dividers, faithful vs. parasitic contrast
description: Three panels separated by thick vertical bars, read left to right. Panel A, 'Original LM Hidden Space', is a 2-D scatter of red, blue, orange and green dots, mixed together, with two crossing axes and a tilted line. Panel B, 'Faithful Intervention Space', has two boxes. One has pink 'Plural Outputs' and blue 'Singular Outputs' regions, with red and blue clusters joined by vertical 'Intervene' arrows. The other has orange 'Masculine' and green 'Feminine' regions, with horizontal 'Intervene' arrows between clusters. Panel C, 'Parasitic Intervention Space', is one box split diagonally into pink and blue regions. Green and orange clusters sit there with intervene arrows that cross between unrelated output regions. Labeled arrows point to the input clusters. Colors tie each cluster to its feature.
caption: A schematic of parasite features for a hypothesized case of syntactic agreement (described in [ref]). A: Prompts in the original high-dimensional DNN hidden space are not basis-aligned by feature. B: By projecting onto subspaces, inputs can be separated by features. Interventions in this space move inputs to the region with corresponding output behavior. C: However, a linear alignment map may connect causally unrelated directions. Interventions in this space create the illusion of causality, despite there being no such relationship in the model. This depicts a parasite feature.\looseness=-1
abstract: Causal Abstraction defines a notion of \emph{equivalence} between a neural network and an algorithm, thus serving as a powerful framework for mechanistic interpretability. In this paper, however, we show the existence of a class of \emph{spurious features} which straightforwardly pass such equivalence tests. Suppose there are two directions in a model's representation space where: (i) one discriminates the input based on some feature, and (ii) the other steers the model towards a certain output. Interpretability methods based on Causal Abstraction (e.g., Distributed Alignment Search) can \emph{spuriously} simulate these directions' combined behavior by leveraging pathways passing through them, giving the impression that the model implements this feature. In such cases, we say the method discovered a \defn{parasite feature}. Experimentally, we show that Distributed Alignment Search finds parasite features using linear alignment maps in two tasks: syntactic agreement and two-digit addition. Our paper highlights an important consideration for Causal Abstraction and contributes to the ongoing debate about best practices for mechanistic interpretability.
